# The problem

TorNet^[Veillette et al., "TorNet: A Benchmark Dataset for Tornado Detection and Prediction
Using Full-Resolution Polarimetric Weather Radar Data," *Artificial Intelligence for the Earth
Systems*, 2024, <https://doi.org/10.1175/AIES-D-24-0006.1>. Code at
<https://github.com/mit-ll/tornet>, weights at
<https://huggingface.co/tornet-ml/tornado_detector_baseline_v1>.] is a tornado detection
benchmark: storm-centered radar chips with a label that says whether a tornado is in them. The
published baseline model looks at one scan and tells you if there's a tornado in it. That's
detection, and detection isn't really what's missing in the last few minutes before a
touchdown. What would help is a signal that shows up before the signature is obvious on the
display.

So the question I'm working on is a prediction one. Every TorNet sample has four consecutive
scans of a storm, about five minutes apart, each with its own label. I give a model the two
oldest scans and ask it, separately, how likely a tornado is in each of the two newest. That's
roughly five and ten minutes after the last thing the model saw.

The framing has to be protected from detection, because a tornado that's already on the radar
is trivial to carry forward. So I only score the model on what I'm calling *pre-onset* cases:
tornado samples where neither input scan is tornadic and the last target scan is. If a tornado
is already visible in an input scan the sample is *ongoing*, reported separately and left out of
the positives. Every non-tornadic sample stays in as a negative. The number then answers "will
one appear", not "will one persist".

The negatives come in three flavors, same as the TorNet paper: all nulls, random non-tornadic
storms, and storms that were under a tornado warning but never produced one. That last group
is the hard case and the headline number everywhere below. Telling a tornadic storm from clear
air is easy; telling it from a warned storm that looked a lot like it is the actual job.

Two reference points turn an AUC into a result. Take the published detector, frozen, run it on
the newest observed scan, and score that against the future labels: that's the *floor*, the
"assume the future looks like the present" baseline, and it's what a forecaster effectively
already has. Run the same detector on the real future scan and you get the *ceiling*: what
detection would give if the forecast were perfect. A model lands somewhere in between, and what
I report is its paired bootstrap difference from the floor on the same files, with a 95%
interval. The floor-to-ceiling gap is the entire prize for forecasting radar, and on one year
it's only about 0.05 to 0.07 AUC.

That small prize plus rare positives sets the limit on what one year can say. There are only
about 200 to 275 pre-onset tornado cases per test year, so a pre-onset AUC carries roughly
±0.025, and a difference under about 0.03 isn't resolvable. Every comparison here is paired,
and more seeds and more years are the only things that shrink the noise.

# The data

TorNet v1.1 is 203,133 samples from 2013 to 2022, released by MIT Lincoln Laboratory under
CC BY 4.0, and already split by the authors into 171,666 train and 31,467 test. 13,857 are
confirmed tornadoes, 64,510 warned storms, 124,766 random storms. A sample is four NEXRAD
dual-pol scans on a polar grid centered on the storm, 120 azimuths by 240 range gates of 250 m
at two tilts, for six products: reflectivity, radial velocity, specific differential phase,
correlation coefficient, differential reflectivity and spectrum width. Each sample also carries
a range-folding mask for the two Doppler products, the four per-scan labels, scan times, the
storm's category and EF rating, the tornado's start and end times, and the chip's azimuth and
range limits.

I repackaged the whole thing on the Hugging Face Hub^[<https://huggingface.co/datasets/jakeryderv/tornet>:
every field as Parquet, 256 samples per shard, one config per year plus a catalog of the scalar
fields. Lossless and verified by reading every shard back and comparing random samples to the
original files exactly.] mostly for a practical reason: the original release is one archive per
year, and I wanted to pick years, partitions and subsets without extracting and re-reading
hundreds of thousands of small netCDF files. A year is now a config, a training set is a list
of years, and a fold is a list of file patterns.

The model sees a scan exactly the way the published detector does. Each product is normalized
to roughly [−1, 1] with the detector's fixed ranges, empty gates get a background value of −3,
the two range-folding channels are appended for fourteen channels total, and two coordinate
channels (range and its inverse) are built from the chip's limits for the detector's CoordConv
layers. Keeping that representation is what lets the published weights drop in as the starting
point with no adapter.

# Setup

The first slice is 2015 only: 19,721 training and 3,902 test samples, 275 pre-onset cases in
the test set. One year is enough to find out whether the idea works at all and cheap enough to
run a lot of variants. All ten years is the obvious next step, and with the data on the Hub it's
a config change.

Validation is held out from the training partition by whole days, 15% of them, never by random
sample. Consecutive samples of one storm are near duplicates, so a random split would let
validation see storms training already memorized and make early stopping meaningless.
Checkpoints are picked on validation AUC and training stops two epochs after the last
improvement.

Loading streams the Parquet shards for the configured years straight from the Hub file cache,
one shard at a time, reshuffling shard order every epoch and rows within each shard. A shard
decompresses to under a gigabyte, so a few loader workers hold a few shards and nothing gets
expanded to disk. The published detector's weights were converted once from the Keras checkpoint
to a plain PyTorch state dict, checked against the original's logits to 2×10^-5^ on the 2013
and 2014 test samples, and published next to the data^[<https://huggingface.co/jakeryderv/tornet-detector-torch>,
MIT like the original.]. A fresh clone needs nothing downloaded by hand.

# The model

I changed as little of the published detector as the question requires. The encoder is the
TorNet CNN as is: four blocks of CoordConv 3×3 layers with 48, 96, 192 and 384 filters, each
block followed by 2×2 max pooling and dropout, ending in a 384-channel map over an 8 × 15 grid
of cells. It runs on both input scans with shared weights, starts from the published weights,
and fine-tunes at a tenth of the head's learning rate. The head is the authors' design too: two
1×1 convs of 512 and 256 channels, a 1×1 conv down to one logit per cell, then the max over
cells, so the map before the max is a spatial likelihood map of where the model thinks the
tornado will be. 4.9M parameters total. One loss: weighted binary cross-entropy of each
horizon's logit against the label of that future scan, with the authors' sample weights, AdamW,
cosine schedule, mixed precision.

What makes it a predictor instead of a detector is where time comes in, and with two scans
that's a modest place. The two feature maps are concatenated cell by cell, so the head's first
layer sees the older and newer features of each cell side by side and can learn any weighted
difference between them: a mesocyclone tightening over five minutes, a reflectivity core moving
in. No recurrence, no attention. With two steps those collapse to the same gated difference at
many times the parameters, and when I tried attention over scans earlier it tied plain
concatenation. What's available is a change detector at the feature level, and that's an honest
description of what two scans allow.

A second combiner makes the time rule explicit instead of learned. With two scans a feature's
history is a line, so each feature can be extrapolated to each horizon as the newest value plus
the per-minute change times that horizon's real lead, read from the scan timestamps instead of
assuming five minutes. One shared head, optionally started from the published head's weights,
reads each extrapolated map. Same expressive power as concat, different inductive bias, and it
actually uses the clock. On top of that there's an optional consistency term that pulls each
extrapolated map toward the encoder's own features of the real future scan (target detached),
which asks for a representation whose trend is predictive without drawing any pixels.

An earlier version carried a lot more machinery: a U-Net decoder that drew the future velocity
and reflectivity, trained with a heat-map-weighted L1 and the frozen detector's cross-entropy on
the drawn chip, as an auxiliary signal for the shared encoder. I dropped it after the comparison
below.

# Baseline and experiments

Everything here is the 2015 test partition, pre-onset cases vs warned storms, paired bootstrap
against the floor in brackets, one seed each.

| horizon | floor | ceiling | with the decoder | encoder + head |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| +5 min | 0.709 | 0.764 | 0.716 (+0.007 [−0.030, +0.040]) | **0.739** (+0.030 [−0.006, +0.064]) |
| +10 min | 0.722 | 0.796 | 0.729 (+0.007 [−0.015, +0.031]) | **0.735** (+0.013 [−0.011, +0.038]) |

: Pre-onset WC AUC on 2015. {#tbl-baseline}

The decoder didn't earn its keep. The plain encoder-and-head model tied it at ten minutes and
beat it at five, +0.023 with an interval of +0.004 to +0.043 on the same files, with half the
parameters and a third less time per epoch. The drawing losses were supposed to help the head
through the shared encoder; on this year they didn't. Both versions overfit after epoch two or
three on a single year of training data, which is why early stopping is in now.

What's left is a modest result, and so far a consistent one. Fine-tuning on the onset target
buys about 0.01 to 0.03 over the published detector on the newest scan, with intervals that
touch zero, and the ceiling stays 0.055 to 0.074 higher. Two radar scans five minutes apart
carry a little of what you'd need to call a tornado ten minutes out, and only a little.

The runs in progress test that reading and the design choices above: the same model under a
second seed, to put a number on seed noise; the extrapolation combiner with and without the
consistency term; then a gentler encoder learning rate against the overfitting and a
frozen-encoder control that asks whether fine-tuning matters at all. Each is a fifteen-minute
run, and their table replaces this paragraph when they land.

# What's next

Two things cap the current numbers, and both are cheap now. Training on eight years instead of
one goes straight at the overfitting and gets the test set to where a few hundredths are
readable. Past that, the ceiling tells you where the rest of the signal *isn't*: even a perfect
radar forecast would add at most 0.07, so the bigger gains have to come from information that
isn't in the chip, like the near-storm environment, and from longer histories than two scans,
where a recurrent combiner would finally have something to recur over.
